unit.title: Use knives for basic task in the kitchen environment

summary: This unit teaches you to choose, handle, use, sharpen, clean and store kitchen knives safely, and to make the basic cuts a cook needs: the classical vegetable cuts, dicing, slicing, chopping and preparing fruit, herbs and Scotch bonnet pepper. You will also learn to set up a safe, hygienic cutting station and what to do when someone is cut.

blocks.p: Every cook in every kitchen, from a villa kitchen in Negril to a large hotel in Montego Bay, starts the day with a knife in the hand. Good knife skills make you faster, safer and tidier, and they save money, because evenly cut food cooks evenly and wastes less. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees, and it is the base for every other cookery unit: you cannot joint a chicken, fillet a fish or prepare vegetables well until you can handle a knife.

Knives cause more cuts in a kitchen than any other tool. Almost all of those cuts come from the same few causes: a blunt knife, a board that slips, a wrong grip, a rush, or a knife in the wrong place. So this unit is about **safety, hygiene and control** as much as about speed and skill.

Slicing, chopping, rocking, dicing and peeling
Keep knives sharp
Hone with a steel before and during work
Sharpen on a whetstone when the edge is dull
Test the edge safely
Make the basic cuts to a given size
Julienne, batonnet, jardinière, paysanne, brunoise, macédoine, chiffonade, tourné and concassé
Dice an onion; mince garlic; chop herbs; prepare Scotch bonnet pepper

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's training kitchen. In the practical tasks you set up a workstation, produce the classical cuts to the sizes on the assessor's card, prepare fruit and seasoning, and sharpen and look after your knives. The assessor watches your safety and hygiene throughout, not only the finished cuts.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: The sizes and settings in this kit are the usual ones. Your Centre's recipe cards, size cards and food safety plan decide the exact figures. If your instructor gives you a different size or a different colour code, use theirs.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A cook who knows the parts of a knife can talk about it, check it for damage and choose the right one. A cook who knows what each knife is for will not use a paring knife to chop a bone or a cleaver to peel a lime.

head: Part
What it is
Why it matters
rows: Point (tip)
The very end of the blade, furthest from the handle.
Used for fine work such as scoring and trimming.
Edge
The sharp lower side of the blade that does the cutting.
Keep it sharp and never test it with your finger.
Heel
The part of the edge nearest the handle.
Used for heavier cuts, such as cutting through thick skin or small bones.
Spine
The blunt top edge of the blade.
Safe to rest your fingers or thumb against when you use the pinch grip.
Bolster
The thick band of metal between the blade and the handle on many forged knives.
Adds weight and balance and protects the hand from slipping onto the blade.
Tang
The part of the blade that goes into the handle. A **full tang** runs the whole length of the handle.
A full tang makes the knife stronger and better balanced.
Rivets
Small metal pins that hold the handle scales onto the tang.
Loose or missing rivets mean the knife is unsafe: report it.
Handle
The part you hold.
Must be clean, dry, undamaged and non-slip.

head: Knife
What it looks like
What it is used for
rows: Cook's (chef's) knife
Broad, tapering blade, about 15 to 30 cm long.
The all-purpose knife: chopping, slicing, dicing, mincing herbs and cutting meat and vegetables.
Paring knife
Short, narrow blade, about 6 to 10 cm.
Peeling and trimming small items, and coring fruit.
Turning (tourné) knife
Short with a curved blade like a bird's beak.
Shaping vegetables into the barrel cut.
Bread (serrated) knife
Long blade with a saw-like edge.
Cutting bread and cakes, and soft or slippery items such as ripe tomatoes.
Boning knife
Narrow, pointed, fairly stiff blade.
Taking bones out of meat and poultry.
Filleting knife
Long, thin, flexible blade.
Taking fish off the bone.
Carving (slicing) knife
Long, narrow blade.
Slicing cooked meat such as roast beef or ham.
Palette knife
Flat, blunt, flexible blade with no cutting edge.
Spreading and lifting. It does not cut.
Cleaver
Heavy, wide, rectangular blade.
Chopping through bones, for example goat for curry goat or oxtail. Use it only on a steady, heavy board.

blocks.note: Using the right knife is safer than using the wrong one. A short knife on a big job, or a blunt knife on a hard job, makes you press harder, and a knife that has to be forced is a knife that slips.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Stainless steel** does not rust easily but can be harder to sharpen. **High-carbon steel** takes a very sharp edge but rusts and stains unless it is dried at once. Many cooks use a high-carbon stainless steel.
**Forged** knives are shaped from one piece of steel, usually have a bolster, and are heavier. **Stamped** knives are cut from a sheet, are lighter and cost less.

Handles are made of plastic, wood or composite. Plastic and composite handles are easier to keep clean. Wooden handles can soak up water and germs, so they should not be soaked or put in a dishwasher.
A good knife feels balanced in your hand: it does not tip towards the blade or the handle.
**Chopping boards:** a board protects the edge and the bench. Cutting on a plate, a metal bench or a tile blunts a knife and makes it slip.
**Sharpening steel (honing steel) and whetstone:** for keeping the edge (see 'Keeping knives sharp').
**Mandoline:** a slicing tool with an adjustable blade in a flat frame. It is very sharp and must always be used with its hand guard.
**Peeler, scissors and scrapers:** for peeling, snipping herbs and scraping the board.

blocks.p: A kitchen is full of people moving fast with hot pots and wet floors. A knife in that space is a danger to you and to everyone near you. These habits protect everyone, and your assessor will watch for every one of them.

head: Situation
What to do
Why
rows: Carrying a knife
Hold it by the handle, **point down**, edge turned back, close to your side. Walk, never run. Say 'Knife behind you' or 'Coming through' when you pass others.
A knife held up or swinging can cut someone who steps in front of you.
Carrying several knives
Carry them in a knife roll or on a tray, with guards on.
Loose knives in the hand can be dropped or can cut you.
Passing a knife
Put it down on the bench for the other person to pick up. Never hand it across, and never throw it.
A knife passed hand to hand can cut either person.
Putting a knife down
Lay it **flat, well away from the edge** of the bench, with the edge turned away from you and others. Never leave it hanging over the edge, under food, peelings or a cloth, or in a sink.
A knife that cannot be seen will be grabbed by mistake.
A knife falls
**Step back and let it fall.** Pick it up only when it has stopped.
Trying to catch it is how deep cuts happen.
Using a knife
Use it only to cut food. Never open tins, prise lids, cut string or tighten screws.
Misuse bends or chips the blade, and a chipped blade is unsafe.
Washing up
Wash each knife on its own, straight away, edge turned away from your hand, and dry it. Never leave knives in the sink.
A hand reaching into soapy water can find a blade it cannot see.

ul: **Keep your mind on the cut.** Look at the knife and the food, not at the person next to you. A moment of distraction causes a cut.
**Keep the blade away from your body and your hands.** Cut away from the hand that holds the food.
**Never hurry.** Speed comes after control, as your skill grows. A rush is when most cuts happen.
**Keep the board steady.** Put a damp cloth or a non-slip mat under it.
**Keep the bench uncluttered** and the floor dry. Wipe up spills, peelings and oil at once, because a slip with a knife in your hand is very dangerous.
**Cut flat.** Make a flat face on round food such as a yam, a pineapple or a melon so that it cannot roll.
**Never use a damaged knife.** A loose handle, a chipped or bent blade or a rusty edge must be reported.
**Cut-resistant glove:** worn on the hand that holds the food when using a mandoline, boning or cutting something hard to grip. It lowers the risk of a cut but does not make a blade harmless.
**Closed, non-slip shoes:** protect your feet from a dropped knife and from slipping.
**Disposable gloves:** for hot peppers, and over a plaster on a cut finger.
**Apron and clean kitchen clothes:** protect you from splashes and the food from you.

blocks.note: Scotch bonnet peppers burn the skin and stay on the hands, the board and the knife. Wear disposable gloves, never touch your eyes or face, and wash the board, the knife and your hands afterwards.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Stop work and put the knife down safely
Press a clean pad on the cut and raise the hand
Small cut: wash it, dry it and cover it with a waterproof blue plaster and a disposable glove
Deep cut or bleeding that will not stop: keep firm pressure on, send for the first-aider and get medical help
Throw away any food, and clean and sanitise anything the blood may have touched
Report it and write it in the accident book

ul: A **blue plaster** is used in kitchens because it shows up if it falls into food.
If a pad is soaked with blood, do not take it off. Put another pad on top and keep pressing.
Report every cut, however small. The accident book is not to blame anyone: it shows what went wrong so it can be stopped from happening again.
In an emergency in Jamaica, call 110 for the fire brigade or an ambulance, and 119 for the police. Follow your workplace's own emergency plan.

blocks.note: Never let a cook who has a bleeding cut carry on cutting food. Food that has blood on it must go in the bin, and the board and knife must be washed and sanitised before anyone uses them again.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Setting up a safe and hygienic cutting station

blocks.p: A good cut starts before the knife touches the food. A cook who sets up well works faster, safer and cleaner, and passes the hygiene part of the practical.

flow: Read the recipe: what is to be cut, to what size, and how much
Wash your hands, put on a clean apron and cover your hair; no jewellery
Wipe the bench and sanitise it
Choose the correct board and set it on a damp cloth or non-slip mat
Choose a clean, sharp knife and the guards or gloves the job needs
Put out a bowl for the cut food and a bowl for waste and trimmings
Wash the produce and bring only what you need to the board

ul: Work at a comfortable height, with your feet apart and your weight on both feet. Stand a little sideways to the bench so that the knife arm has room.
Keep the board a hand's width from the edge of the bench, so the food cannot roll off.
Keep the food, the bowls and the knife in a line from left to right (or right to left, if you are left-handed) so you do not reach across the blade.
Wipe the board between jobs so that peelings and juice do not build up.

blocks.p: Colour-coded boards keep raw food and ready-to-eat food apart, so that germs on raw meat do not pass to salad. This is **cross-contamination**. The usual colour code is below, but kitchens differ, so always follow your Centre's code.

head: Colour (usual)
Used for
rows: Red
Raw meat
Blue
Raw fish and seafood
Yellow
Cooked meat (some kitchens use it for raw poultry)
Green
Salad and fruit
Brown
Root vegetables, such as yam and potatoes
White
Bakery and dairy items

ul: A board with deep cuts holds food and germs. Replace worn and cracked boards, and scrub them well.
Do not use one board for raw chicken and then for salad. If you must change from one food to another, wash and sanitise the board and knife first.
Wash and sanitise your hands between raw and ready-to-eat foods.
Wooden boards are used in some kitchens but must be scrubbed and dried well; follow your Centre's rules.

blocks.p: Some guests are allergic to foods such as nuts, shellfish, fish, eggs, milk, soya, wheat (gluten) and sesame. Cutting a nut and then a salad on the same board and knife can pass the allergen on. Wash and sanitise the board and knife between foods when the order has an allergy, and tell the chef at once if you are unsure.

ul: Wash your hands with soap and warm water before starting, after the toilet, after touching raw food, your face, hair or phone, after handling waste, and after any break.
Keep your nails short and clean, with no nail polish.
Wear a clean uniform, apron and hair cover. Remove rings, bracelets and watches.
Cover cuts with a waterproof blue plaster and a glove.
Do not come to work with vomiting, diarrhoea or an infected wound. Tell your supervisor.
Hold a Food Handler's Permit from the health department, as the law in Jamaica requires for food handlers.

blocks.p: Two hands work together: one holds the knife, the other holds the food. Learn both grips well. Most cuts happen because the food hand is in the wrong place.

blocks.h: Holding the knife: the pinch grip

blocks.p: Hold the handle with the last three fingers. Pinch the blade, just in front of the bolster, between your thumb and the side of your first finger. This gives control over the blade. A cook who holds only the handle has much less control.

ul: Keep the grip firm but relaxed. Gripping too hard tires the hand.
For small tasks (paring a fruit in the hand, trimming a pepper) hold the knife like a pencil, with the blade turned away from you.

head: Grip
How you do it
When you use it
rows: Claw grip
Curl your fingertips under, thumb tucked behind. Your knuckles face the knife, and the side of the blade rests lightly against them as you cut. Move the hand back a little after each cut.
Slicing and dicing. It keeps your fingertips out of the way and gives even slices.
Bridge grip
Place the food on its flat side. Arch your fingers and thumb over it, like a bridge. The knife passes through the gap, under the arch.
Cutting round or hard items in half, such as a tomato, an onion, a lime or a potato.
Flat palm (never)
A flat palm with stretched fingers on the food.
Never use this for cutting. The fingertips are in the path of the blade.

blocks.note: A cook who holds food with straight fingers will, sooner or later, cut a fingertip. Curl the fingers under for every slice.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Action
How it works
Use it for
rows: Slicing
Draw the blade forward and down through the food, using the whole length of the edge in a smooth sawing movement. Do not press down.
Meat, bread, tomatoes, onions and fruit.
Push cut
Push the blade forward and down through the food, with the tip on the board.
Firm vegetables, such as carrots and celery, when slicing and dicing.
Rocking (chopping)
Keep the tip of the knife on the board and raise and lower the heel, with the other hand's fingers on the back of the blade near the tip. Move the knife over the pile.
Chopping and mincing herbs, garlic and onions finely.
Chopping through bone
Use a cleaver on a heavy, steady board. Hold the food away from the blade and strike firmly in one stroke. Never hold the food with your hand in the path of the blow.
Bones, as in curry goat and oxtail.
Peeling
Use a peeler or paring knife, always moving the blade **away from your body and the hand that holds the food**. Peel over the waste bowl.
Carrots, cho cho, pumpkin, yam, mangoes and pineapples.
Scoring
Make shallow cuts in the surface with the point of the knife.
Fish, chicken, mango cheeks, pineapple eyes and the base of tomatoes.

ul: Give every round item a **flat base** first, by slicing a thin piece off one side, so it cannot roll.
Cut with the **tip of the knife near or on the board**. Never lift the blade high above the board.
Cut small and soft items on a board, not in the hand.
Do not cut towards your hand. Turn the food, not the blade.
Never cut on the bench top, a plate or a tray: the knife slips and goes blunt.
Let the knife do the work. If you must push hard, the knife is blunt, or you are using the wrong one.

blocks.p: A **sharp knife is a safe knife**. It goes through food with little force and does not slip. A blunt knife needs a hard push, skids off the skin of a tomato or a yam and causes injuries. It also crushes food and makes ragged cuts.

head: Compare
Honing with a steel
Sharpening on a whetstone
rows: What it does
Straightens and realigns the edge, which bends over a little with use. It takes off almost no metal.
Grinds away metal to make a new edge when the knife is dull.
How often
Often: before each job and during a long job.
Only when honing no longer brings the edge back. This may be every few weeks or months, depending on use.
Equipment
A sharpening (honing) steel
A whetstone, usually a coarse side and a fine side

flow: Hold the steel firmly, point down on a steady board or on a damp cloth, or in the air at a safe distance from your body
Place the heel of the knife against the top of the steel at an angle of about 15 to 20 degrees
Draw the knife down and across the steel, from heel to tip
Do the same on the other side, with the same number of strokes
Repeat a few times, then wipe the blade and test it

ul: Keep the angle the same all the way. The angle is the same as the angle on the edge of the knife; follow the maker's advice.
Keep your fingers behind the guard of the steel and the edge of the knife pointing away from you.
Light, even strokes are best. Pressing hard does not help.

flow: Soak the stone in water, or wet it, as the maker says
Set the stone on a damp cloth or a stone holder so it cannot slip
Hold the knife at about 15 to 20 degrees to the stone, as the maker's guide says
Push the edge across the stone, from heel to tip, with light pressure, in a smooth sweep, again and again
Do the same number of strokes on the other side
Move from the coarse side to the fine side to polish the edge
Wash, dry and test the knife

ul: Always sharpen the same way. A changing angle makes a rounded, blunt edge.
Wash the knife well after sharpening, because the metal dust and the stone's grit can get on the blade.
Do not sharpen knives with a serrated edge on a flat stone. They need a special rod or a specialist.
Slice a ripe tomato or a piece of paper. A sharp knife goes through with little pressure.
**Never test the edge on your finger or thumb.**
A dull edge may also reflect the light as a thin, bright line when you look at it: a sharp edge does not shine.

blocks.note: Never carry out sharpening in a rush or at a busy time. Keep the steel and stone steady, keep your fingers well behind the edge and never hone towards your hand.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Store clean, dry knives in a **knife block, a magnetic rack, a knife roll or a sheath**, with the edges protected.
Never store knives loose in a drawer, in a bucket of water or on the bench under a cloth.
Keep knives dry. Water and food acids stain and rust blades. Dry high-carbon steel at once.
Do not put good knives in a dishwasher: heat and detergent damage the handle and the edge.
Check each knife for damage when you take it out and when you put it away. Report problems.

blocks.p: Cuts have names so that every cook in the kitchen, and every recipe, means the same thing. **Cutting food to the same size and shape** makes it cook evenly, so the small pieces are not mushy while the big ones are raw. It also looks neat and helps you control portion size and cost.

head: Cut
What it looks like
Usual size
Typical use
rows: Julienne
Thin strips like matchsticks.
About 2 mm × 2 mm × 40 mm (fine julienne is about 1 mm)
Garnish, stir-fry, salads.
Batonnet
Thicker sticks.
About 6 mm × 6 mm × 50 mm
Raw vegetable sticks, chips and cooked vegetables.
Jardinière
Short, thick sticks, a little bigger than julienne.
About 4 mm × 4 mm × 20 mm
Vegetables served with a main dish; some soups.
Paysanne
Thin, flat shapes, such as squares or rounds.
About 1 cm × 1 cm × 2 mm
Country-style soups and stews.
Brunoise
Tiny, even dice.
About 3 mm cubes (fine brunoise is about 1.5 mm)
Garnish for soups and sauces.
Macédoine
Small dice.
About 5 mm cubes
Mixed vegetables or fruit.
Large, medium and small dice
Even cubes.
About 20 mm, 12 mm and 6 mm
Stews, soups and roasting.
Mirepoix
Rough-cut onion, carrot and celery; size matches the cooking time.
Rough pieces
Flavour base for stocks and braises. The vegetables are strained out.
Chiffonade
Fine ribbons of leaf.
Roll the leaves, slice across at about 2 to 3 mm
Basil, callaloo, lettuce and mint as a garnish.
Tourné
A small barrel shape with seven curved sides.
About 5 cm long
Elegant potato and carrot garnishes.
Concassé
Tomato that is peeled, seeded and diced.
Dice of about 5 to 10 mm
Sauces, garnishes and salads.

blocks.note: Sizes in textbooks differ by a millimetre or two. Your Centre's size card, which the assessor shows you, is the one to follow in your practical. Measure a sample against a ruler.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Cutting a carrot into julienne and brunoise

flow: Wash the carrot and peel it; trim the ends
Cut it into pieces about 5 cm long
Square off one side so the piece lies flat and does not roll; trim the other three sides to make a neat block
Slice the block lengthways into thin, even planks about 2 mm thick (claw grip)
Stack two or three planks and slice them into strips of the same width: this is julienne
Gather the julienne into a bundle and cut across it at the same width to make brunoise
Check the sizes with a ruler, and keep the trimmings for stock
Cut the onion in half through the root, using the bridge grip, and peel it
Lay it flat side down, with the root away from you
Cut thin slices towards the root, but not through it, so the layers are held together
If the onion is big, cut flat slices parallel to the board, across the layers, again leaving the root end
Turn the onion and slice across, with the claw grip, to make even dice
Keep the root end for the stockpot

ul: Leaving the root on holds the layers together as you cut.
A sharp knife cuts the cells cleanly and makes fewer tears. Cold onions also make fewer fumes.

flow: Cut out the core, and score a shallow X in the base
Lower the tomato into boiling water for about 10 to 15 seconds
Lift it out into iced water so it stops cooking
Peel off the skin, starting from the X
Cut it into quarters and remove the seeds and the core
Dice the flesh to the size needed

blocks.note: Take care with the boiling water. Lower the tomato in with a slotted spoon, and use dry oven cloths for the pot.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Wash fruit and vegetables before you peel or cut them, so that soil and germs on the skin are not carried into the flesh by the knife. Cut fruit for a platter on a clean green board with a clean knife, and keep it covered and chilled.

head: Fruit
How to prepare it
rows: Pineapple
Wash it; cut off the top and the base so it stands flat
Stand it up and cut the skin off in strips from top to bottom, following the curve
Remove the 'eyes' with the point of the knife in spiral lines
Cut it into quarters lengthways, cut out the hard core, then slice
Mango
Hold it upright; slice down each side of the flat stone to take off the two 'cheeks'
Score the flesh in a grid without cutting through the skin
Push the skin inside out, or slice the flesh away from the skin
Pawpaw (papaya)
Peel it with a peeler or paring knife
Cut it in half lengthways, scoop out the seeds with a spoon
Slice or cut it into wedges or cubes
Watermelon
Cut a slice off one end so it stands steady
Cut it in half, then into wedges, or cut away the rind and cut the flesh into cubes
Take the seeds out if the recipe says
Oranges and limes
Cut off the ends, stand the fruit up, and slice the peel and pith off from top to bottom
For segments, cut between the membranes
Halve limes with the bridge grip and cut against the board
Avocado (pear)
Cut round the stone lengthways, twist the halves apart and remove the stone
Scoop out the flesh with a spoon and slice
Squeeze lime juice over it to keep it from browning

ul: Always put a flat cut surface on the board before you cut downwards.
Cut fruit just before it is needed, to keep it fresh, or cover and chill it. Lime or lemon juice slows browning on apple, banana and avocado.
Keep the peelings and seeds in a bowl for waste, and sweep them from the board often.

**Ground provisions (yam, sweet potato, dasheen, coco):** wash well, peel with a sharp knife or peeler, and cut a flat base on the piece so it sits steady. Raw yam can be slippery and some can irritate the skin, so dry your hands and wear gloves if your skin is sensitive. Put cut pieces in cold water to stop them going dark.
**Cho cho and pumpkin:** halve them with the bridge grip, then use a heavy cook's knife. Hard pumpkin should be cut with the cut face down so it cannot slide.
**Callaloo and leafy greens:** wash well, strip the leaves from the stem, stack, roll tightly and slice into a chiffonade. Chop the stems small, as they take longer to cook.
**Carrots, cucumbers and celery:** square off, then slice and cut as the recipe says.
**Tomatoes:** use a sharp serrated or paring knife. A dull knife crushes them.
**Cabbage:** quarter it, cut out the core and slice thinly across the leaves.

blocks.h: Herbs, garlic and Scotch bonnet pepper

head: Item
Method
Care
rows: Thyme
Strip the small leaves from the woody stem by running your fingers down it; use the leaves whole or chop them. Do not use the stems unless the recipe says.
Wash and dry before chopping.
Scallion (escallion)
Trim the roots, wash well, and slice thinly across, or chop the white and green parts.
Wash well, as soil collects between the layers.
Garlic
Crush a clove under the flat of the blade to loosen the skin, peel it, then chop it and mince it by rocking the knife over it.
Wash your hands and board after, because the smell stays.
Parsley and other soft herbs
Gather into a tight bunch, curl your fingers into the claw grip and chop with a rocking action. Keep the herbs dry, because wet herbs smear.
Use a very sharp knife so that the leaves are cut, not bruised.
Scotch bonnet pepper
Wear gloves. Cut off the stem, halve the pepper, and scrape out the seeds and white membrane with the knife point or a spoon for less heat. Slice or chop as needed.
Wash the board and knife, and your hands, afterwards. Never touch your eyes.

blocks.note: For jerk seasoning, brown stew and green seasoning, the Scotch bonnet is the hottest part of the work. If you touch your eyes by mistake, rinse them gently with plenty of clean, cool water for several minutes and tell your supervisor. Oil, not water, helps remove the heat from the skin, so wash the oil off with soap afterwards.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Peel thinly: a thick peel wastes food that you have paid for.

Use the whole vegetable. Save clean, sound trimmings (onion and carrot ends, celery leaves, herb stalks, mushroom stalks) for the **stockpot**. Do not keep peelings that are dirty or have been on the floor.
Cut sizes to the recipe, so you do not trim away good food to make it fit.
Weigh a sample of the waste to see how much you are throwing away. Your supervisor uses this to work out costs.

sections.title: Cleaning, storing and finishing the task

flow: Wash the knife straight after use, so food cannot dry on it
Hold it by the handle, edge away from your hand, and wash it in warm, soapy water with a cloth or brush
Rinse it
Sanitise it with a food-safe sanitiser, for the contact time on the label
Dry it from spine to edge, with the edge turned away from your hand, or leave it to air dry in a rack
Put it away in the block, rack or roll

ul: **Wash one knife at a time.** Never put several in the sink together.
**Wash and sanitise boards** after every job, stand them on their edge to air dry, and check them for deep cuts.
After raw chicken, meat, fish or Scotch bonnet pepper, wash and sanitise the knife and board **before** the next food.
Wash your hands after cleaning up.
Put all waste in the right bin and keep trimmings for stock.
Wipe the bench with hot detergent water and sanitise it.
Sweep and wipe the floor so that no peelings are left to slip on.
Return all clean equipment to its place.
Put cut food in clean, covered containers, label it with its name and the date, and store it in the fridge at 5 °C or below.
Cut vegetables keep best covered and chilled; cut ground provisions and potatoes are kept in cold water in the fridge.
Use the oldest stock first: first in, first out.
Do not leave cut food on the bench for longer than the job needs.
Report a damaged knife, a worn board or a faulty mandoline to your supervisor.
Report every cut, and write it in the accident book: who, what, when, what happened and what was done.
Tell your supervisor if a knife is missing. A missing knife may be in the food.

blocks.note: A cut or an accident is not a mark against you for reporting it. It is a mark against you for hiding it. An unreported cut can become infected, can put blood in food, and the cause is never put right.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: name the parts of a knife (point, edge, heel, spine, bolster, tang, rivets, handle)
say what a cook's, paring, bread, boning, filleting, carving and turning knife and a cleaver are used for
explain why a sharp knife is safer than a blunt one
carry a knife point down by my side, pass it by laying it on the bench, and put it down flat away from the edge
explain why I step back and let a falling knife fall
explain why knives are never left in the sink
set up a cutting station with the correct board on a damp cloth, bowls for food and waste, and a clean knife
give the usual board colours and explain cross-contamination
use the pinch grip, the claw grip and the bridge grip, and say when each is used
slice, push cut, rock and peel safely
hone a knife on a steel at about 15 to 20 degrees and sharpen it on a whetstone
test an edge without touching it
make julienne, batonnet, jardinière, paysanne, brunoise, macédoine, chiffonade, tourné and concassé to the sizes on the card
dice an onion and mince garlic and herbs
prepare a pineapple, mango, pawpaw and watermelon with a knife
wear gloves and take care when cutting Scotch bonnet pepper
give first aid for a small cut, and know what to do for a deep one
clean, sanitise, dry and store knives and boards correctly
save clean trimmings for stock and keep waste low
report every cut and write it in the accident book

terms: The all-purpose knife for chopping, slicing and dicing.
A small knife for peeling and trimming.
A narrow, pointed knife for taking bones out of meat.
A thin, flexible knife for taking fish off the bone.
A heavy knife for chopping through bones.
With a saw-like edge, as on a bread knife.
The blunt back edge of the blade.
The sharp cutting side of the blade.
The part of the edge nearest the handle.
The thick band of metal between the blade and the handle.
The end of the blade that goes into the handle; a full tang runs the full length.
Holding the blade between thumb and finger, just in front of the handle.
Holding food with the fingertips curled under, knuckles guiding the blade.
Holding food with an arch of fingers and thumb, with the knife passing under the arch.
A chopping action with the tip on the board and the heel moving up and down.
Straightening the edge with a steel.

A slicing tool with a sharp adjustable blade; use it only with its guard.
Thin strips like matchsticks, about 2 mm × 2 mm × 40 mm.
Short sticks about 4 mm × 4 mm × 20 mm.
Thin, flat pieces about 1 cm across and 2 mm thick.
Fine ribbons made from rolled leaves.
A small barrel shape with seven curved sides.

Rough-cut onion, carrot and celery used for flavour.
Cutting food into very small, fine pieces.

c1.title: A busy lunch at a guesthouse in Negril
c1.text: Chef Marcia runs the kitchen of a small guesthouse in Negril. At 11:30 a.m. the lunch orders start. Her new trainee, Kemar, has set a wooden board on the stainless steel bench with no cloth under it, and it slides when he cuts. His cook's knife has not been sharpened for weeks, and he has pushed down hard on a tomato, which crushed instead of slicing. A few minutes later he picks up his knife, turns to speak to a waiter and walks across the kitchen with the knife held out in front of him.

c2.title: Sharpening practical at the training kitchen in Kingston
c2.text: In the Centre's kitchen in Kingston, trainee Shanice is told to bring back the edge on a dull cook's knife. She has a sharpening steel and a whetstone. Her classmate Delroy says, 'Just push the knife straight across the stone at a steep angle: it is quicker.' Shanice's instructor reminds her that the knife maker recommends about 15 to 20 degrees.

c3.title: A fruit platter for a wedding in Ocho Rios
c3.text: Trainee Akeem is preparing a fruit platter for 60 guests at a wedding in Ocho Rios. He has pineapples, ripe mangoes, a large watermelon and some limes. He washes his hands and the fruit. The pineapple and the watermelon roll about on the board. The platter must be ready two hours before the guests arrive, and the kitchen is warm. Akeem has only one board, which is red, and he has just finished jointing a tray of raw chicken on it for tonight's dinner.

c4.title: Vegetable cuts for a catering order in Mandeville
c4.text: A caterer in Mandeville gives trainee Camille an order card: carrot julienne, a brunoise of cho cho, diced onion and tomato concassé for a soup garnish. Camille cuts the carrots into sticks but they are of very different sizes. Her chef says that vegetables cut to different sizes will not cook evenly. Later she must cut Scotch bonnet pepper for a pepper sauce for the same job.

c5.title: A cut finger at the carving station in Montego Bay
c5.text: At a hotel in Montego Bay, cook Roy is slicing cooked ham for the buffet when the knife slips and cuts the top of his finger. It bleeds slightly into the sliced ham on the board. Another cook offers to wrap his finger in the side towel so that he can finish the job quickly. The supervisor, Ms. Wright, arrives.

questions.q: What is the main danger of Kemar's board sliding on the bench?
o: The knife may slip off the food and cut him or someone close by
The board will wear out much more quickly on a steel bench
The food will be cut into pieces of very uneven sizes
The knife edge will lose its sharpness faster on the board
questions.why: A board that moves makes the knife slip. A damp cloth or non-slip mat under the board holds it steady. Uneven pieces and a worn edge are minor problems next to a cut.

questions.q: Why did the tomato crush instead of slice?
o: The tomato was too ripe and too cold for any knife to slice
The knife was blunt, and so needed pressure that crushed the skin
A cook's knife is the wrong shape for cutting any soft fruit
He cut with the tip, when he should have used the heel
questions.why: A blunt knife crushes soft food and needs hard pressure, which also makes it slip. Keep the edge honed and sharp; a serrated knife also helps on ripe tomatoes.

questions.q: Kemar's walk across the kitchen was unsafe. What is the safest way for him to move his knives to the far bench?
o: Hold them together in one fist, with the points facing the floor
Lay them on a tray, or roll them in a knife roll, with guards on
Carry each one under his arm, wrapped in a clean side towel
Slide them along the bench one at a time, away from the edge
questions.why: A knife roll, or a tray with the knives guarded, keeps the edges covered if he trips or someone bumps him. Knives held loose in the hand, tucked under an arm or slid along a bench can cut him or others.

questions.q: Kemar is called away in the middle of a cut. What should he do with the knife?
o: Rest it across the top of the board so that it is within reach
Lay it flat on the bench, well away from the edge, edge away from him
Push it under the edge of a cloth, so that it is out of the way
Leave it in the sink with the dirty pots until he returns
questions.why: A knife left flat and visible, away from the edge, will not be knocked off or grabbed by mistake. A knife under a cloth or in a sink is hidden and gets people cut.

questions.q: What does honing a knife on a steel actually do?
o: It straightens the edge that has bent over with use
It grinds away a thick layer of metal to make a new edge
It removes rust and food stains from the whole blade
It makes the blade stronger so that it stays sharp for months
questions.why: Honing realigns the edge and takes off almost no metal; it is done often. Grinding a new edge is sharpening, done on a whetstone only when the knife is dull.

questions.q: Why should Shanice ignore Delroy's advice to use a steep angle?
o: A steep angle needs more water on the stone to work well
A steep angle makes the stone wear out much faster than usual
A steep angle makes a thick, blunt edge that cuts poorly
A steep angle makes the knife too sharp to use on food
questions.why: A steep angle gives a thick, wide edge that does not cut well. About 15 to 20 degrees, held the same all the way, gives a thin, keen edge. Follow the knife maker's advice.

questions.q: How can Shanice test the sharpened edge most safely?
o: Run her thumb gently along the edge to feel for sharpness
Press the edge against her fingernail to see if it catches
Slice through a ripe tomato or a sheet of paper with it
Tap the edge on the steel to hear whether it rings clear
questions.why: A sharp knife slices a tomato or paper with little pressure. Never test an edge on your skin or nail: it is how cuts happen.

questions.q: After sharpening, what should Shanice do before she uses the knife on food?
o: Wash and dry the knife to remove the metal dust and grit
Wipe it once on her apron to take the dust off it
Oil the blade lightly so that it does not rust in the humid air
Leave it wet on the stone so that the edge stays smooth
questions.why: Sharpening leaves fine metal and grit on the blade. Wash it, rinse it and dry it carefully before it touches food.

questions.q: What is the safest way for Akeem to stop the pineapple and watermelon rolling?
o: Hold each one tightly with his free hand while he cuts down
Slice off a thin piece to make a flat base, and stand it on it
Cut them while they lie on their sides, rolling them as he goes
Wedge each one against the wall of a bowl as he cuts
questions.why: A flat base makes round fruit stable, so the knife goes down through it and not across your hand. Holding a rolling fruit or cutting towards your hand risks a deep cut.

questions.q: What should Akeem do about using the red board for the fruit?
o: Use it after wiping it with a dry cloth to take off the crumbs
Use the other side of the board, since it has not touched chicken
Use it if he rinses it with cold water and the fruit is washed
Wash and sanitise it first, or use a clean green board
questions.why: Raw chicken carries germs that can pass to ready-to-eat fruit. A board used for raw meat must be washed with detergent and sanitised before it is used for fruit, or a clean board of the right colour should be used.

questions.q: The cut fruit will wait two hours in a warm kitchen. What should Akeem do?
o: Spread it on the platter now and cover it with a dry cloth
Pile it in a bowl on the bench and stir it from time to time
Cover the platter and keep it chilled until it is served
Squeeze lime juice on it and leave it near the window
questions.why: Cut fruit is ready to eat and can grow germs in a warm kitchen. Covered and chilled at 5 °C or below keeps it safe and fresh. Lime juice only slows browning.

questions.q: Akeem cuts a mango. Which method wastes the least flesh?
o: Peel it with a paring knife, then cut slices off all round the stone
Slice down each side of the flat stone to take off two cheeks, then score them
Chop it through the stone into large pieces and scoop out the flesh
Cut it across the middle and squeeze out the flesh by hand
questions.why: Cutting off the two 'cheeks' either side of the flat stone gives clean pieces of fruit that are easy to score and serve. Peeling a slippery mango in the hand is also how many cuts happen.

questions.q: Why does the chef want Camille's carrot sticks cut to the same size?
o: So that all the pieces cook evenly and the dish looks neat
So that the carrots stay crisp for longer in the fridge
So that the knife stays sharper for longer between honings
So that fewer carrots are needed to fill the soup pot
questions.why: Equal pieces cook in the same time. Mixed sizes leave small pieces overcooked and large pieces hard. Neat cuts also help with portion control and presentation.

questions.q: Camille is to cut the carrot into julienne first. What is the size of a typical julienne?
o: About 6 mm square and 50 mm long
About 2 mm square and 40 mm long
About 5 mm cubes, all the same size
About 3 mm cubes, all the same size
questions.why: Julienne is matchstick-thin: about 2 mm × 2 mm × 40 mm. Sticks of 6 mm are batonnet; 3 mm cubes are brunoise and 5 mm cubes are macédoine. Check the Centre's size card.

questions.q: She now needs a tomato concassé. Which steps are in the right order?
o: Peel, score the base, dice, then blanch in boiling water
Dice, score the base, blanch, then peel the cubes
Score the base, blanch briefly, cool in iced water, peel, seed, dice
Blanch, score the base, peel, dice, then remove the seeds
questions.why: Scoring an X lets the skin split in the hot water. A short blanch loosens the skin, iced water stops the cooking, and then you peel, seed and dice.

questions.q: Camille prepares the Scotch bonnet pepper. What is the best way to protect herself and the next job?
o: Wear disposable gloves, and wash the board and knife and her hands after
Work quickly without gloves, and wash her hands in cold water at the end
Wear a cut-resistant glove, then use the same knife on the onions
Keep her gloves on while she rubs her eyes with the back of her hand
questions.why: Capsaicin sticks to skin, boards and knives, and burns the eyes. Disposable gloves protect the hands; washing the board and knife stops it passing to the next food. A cut-resistant glove is for blades, not for pepper.

questions.q: What should the supervisor, Ms. Wright, tell Roy to do first?
o: Rinse the cut under the tap, and carry on slicing the ham
Wrap the side towel tightly round it, and return to work
Stop work, put the knife down, and press a clean pad on the cut
Put a glove over the cut, and carry on as before
questions.why: Stop work and put the knife down safely first. Then press a clean pad on the cut. Only a minor cut is then cleaned and covered with a blue plaster and a glove; the side towel is never clean enough.

questions.q: What must be done with the sliced ham that has blood on it?
o: Rinse it under cold running water and serve it as normal
Cook it again so that the heat kills any germs in the blood
Cut off the part with blood and serve the rest of the slices
Throw it away, then wash and sanitise the board and knife
questions.why: Blood can carry germs, and you cannot be sure how far it has spread. Throw away the food, then wash and sanitise everything it touched. Rinsing or reheating ready-to-eat food is not enough.

questions.q: A cook says, 'I only hone my knife when it will not cut a tomato.' What should you tell him?
o: That is right, because honing removes a lot of metal from the edge
Hone it every few minutes, as honing makes no difference otherwise
Hone it often, as it straightens the edge before it gets dull
Never hone it, since only a stone can sharpen a blade
questions.why: The edge bends over with use, and a quick hone keeps it straight, so the knife stays sharp longer and needs the stone much less often. Honing removes almost no metal.

questions.q: Which cut is made by rolling up leaves, such as callaloo or basil, and slicing them across into fine ribbons?
o: Paysanne
Chiffonade
Concassé
Mirepoix
questions.why: Chiffonade is fine ribbons of leaf made by rolling and slicing. Paysanne is a thin flat shape, concassé is peeled and seeded tomato, and mirepoix is rough-cut onion, carrot and celery.
